opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the internet arrived at a moment when I was a fairly curious kid but didn't really have many people around me to talk to about the things I was interested in. So the first feeling was that the walls of the classroom suddenly disappeared. You could follow a question as far as you wanted, and nobody told you to stop because it wasn't on the exam.

What I remember most is the forums and the personal websites. There was a very hands-on culture back then. If you wanted a homepage, you learned some HTML. If you wanted it to look good, you learned a bit of design. If you wanted it to do something, you learned to program. Learning didn't feel like studying. It felt like building things because you wanted them to exist. I think that shaped a lot of how I approach research even now: you learn by making things, and you figure out the theory along the way.

The expression side mattered just as much. On the internet nobody knew how old you were or which school you went to. If you posted something interesting, people responded to the idea itself. For a teenager that was very empowering. It gave me the sense that ideas could stand on their own, and that you could join a conversation with people far more experienced than you if you had something real to contribute.

Looking back, it was also a kind of early training in open communities. Later, in research, I found the same spirit in open-source code, arXiv, and people discussing papers online. It was the same feeling I had as a kid on those forums: knowledge is something you share, and the community gets stronger because people put their work out in the open. That's something I still care a lot about.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes posting online and joining conversations, but does not identify this as a shift beyond one-way learning through reading.

fable-5.1.text:
I grew up in a small city in China, and honestly, before the internet, the world felt very bounded. What you knew was what your teachers knew, what was in the library, what your parents could tell you. So when I first got online, around middle school, it was a shock in the best way. Suddenly I could read about things nobody around me cared about or even knew existed.

I remember spending hours on forums, on BBS boards, just reading. People were arguing about programming languages, about philosophy, about music. And the thing that struck me was that nobody cared who you were. You could be a kid in a provincial city and post a question, and someone from Beijing or from the US would answer you seriously. That was very liberating. Your ideas mattered more than your background.

It also changed how I expressed myself. In school you write what the teacher wants. Online, I started writing things because I actually wanted to say them. I kept a blog for a while, mostly about technical stuff I was learning, and some of it was pretty bad. But writing publicly forced me to think clearly. If you say something wrong, someone will tell you, sometimes not very politely. That feedback loop taught me a lot about how to reason and how to communicate.

And I think that experience shaped how I approach research later. The open-source culture, putting your code and your ideas out there, letting people poke at them. That felt natural to me because it was how I learned in the first place. The internet taught me that knowledge is something you participate in, not just something you receive.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes moving from hours of reading forums to writing publicly on a blog to share what they wanted to say, clearly identifying a shift from reading to publishing their own views online.

astra-6.text:
For me, the internet opened up a way to follow my curiosity. In a classroom, there’s usually a sequence: this is what you learn today, and that’s what comes next. Online, you could start with one question, find something you didn’t understand, and keep following it. You didn’t have to wait for someone to introduce a subject to you.

And learning and expressing yourself became connected. You could put a thought into words, share it, and get a response. That process makes you ask, “Do I actually understand what I’m saying?” So the internet wasn’t just a place to receive information. It was also a place to develop your own voice through that exchange.

r001.rationale: It describes putting a thought into words and sharing it online to get a response, contrasting that exchange with merely receiving information.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the internet opened up a way to learn beyond what was available in the classroom. You could follow your curiosity, find people interested in the same questions, and see how they approached a problem. Learning became something you could actively pursue rather than just receive.

And expression was connected to that. You could share an idea before it was fully formed, get feedback, and refine your thinking. That was exciting—the sense that you could participate in a conversation, not just watch it.

r001.rationale: The response describes sharing an idea online and participating in a conversation, but it does not connect this shift to one-way learning through reading.
